endorsements.quote: A workable model includes a multidisciplinary review group with radiology clinical leadership, imaging informatics, information technology, quality and safety, compliance or privacy, cybersecurity, operations, and representatives from the user group affected by the tool.
First, there is a single intake path.
The depth of review should then increase with risk.
Third, there is named ownership at multiple levels.
Map current and future-state workflow; identify who acts on AI output

A useful objective is specific: reduce time to first radiologist review for positive non-contrast head CT examinations, reduce report omissions in a defined workflow, or improve time to diagnosis for a targeted cohort.
The scorecard should change with the use case.
That means collecting structured user feedback, review ing failure modes, monitoring for changes in performance, and being willing to modify or retire tools that no longer deliver enough value.

Launch one to two selected use cases end to end using the shared process.

A practical call to action is therefore not to pretend every integration can be standard on day one, but to standardise the integration process: common interface intake, reusable routing patterns, consistent logging, downtime procedures, cybersecurity review, and documentation of where AI output enters the clinical workflow.
What action is expected: reprioritise, acknowledge, document, communicate, or ignore unless discrepant?
Define feedback channels and postdeployment review plan

unlisted_practices: Establish a minimum shared governance structure before the first AI use cases enter deployment.
Define a fallback workflow for when an AI tool is unavailable, delayed, or wrong.
Define retirement or stop criteria for each AI use case before deployment.

Adopt a two-speed operating model matching review intensity to risk, with a fast lane for low-risk use cases and a clinical safety lane for AI affecting prioritisation, interpretation, reporting, or patient management.
Standardise AI integration processes (common intake, logging, downtime plan, cybersecurity review, support model) rather than treating each deployment as a blank sheet.
Define SMART-style clinical intent for each AI use case with population, measurable baseline, intended action, responsible user, and time-bound target.
Use use-case-specific metrics such as time-to-action, false escalation rate, and workflow measures rather than model accuracy alone to assess AI value.
Review live performance after launch and decide to scale, modify, or stop each AI tool using a common scorecard.

screen.reason: Editorial presenting a practical six-part framework and 90-day roadmap for governance, workflow orchestration, and operational deployment of AI in radiology.
